messages.subject: Re: g(0) in aerial surveys
messages.body_plain:
None of your suggestions address g(0).  You can't assess g(0) without
additional information such as what you gain with independent observers
or with marked animals.  In your case, independent observers is unlikely
to help because birds that aren't visible won't be visible to either
observer.  The only solution that seems feasible is radio-telemetry.

messages.subject: Re: g(0) in aerial surveys
messages.body_plain:
If you include the distance to the moose in your sightability GLM and
then predict sightability at distance 0, that is g(0).  It can be
habitat specific as long as you have enough data to estimate density and
detection probability by habitat.

It is preferable to estimate g(0) concurrent with the collection of the
distance sampling data by having telemetered animals available for
sighting during the course of the survey.  Then g(0) is more applicable
to the conditions under which the survey was conducted.  I believe some
of these issues are discussed in the symposium volume Garner et al
Marine Mammal Survey and Assessment Methods and in ch6 of the adv
distance sampling book.

--jeff

messages.subject: g(0) in aerial surveys
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

We are using Distance Sampling for existing aerial moose survey data.
The
problem is that the surveyed area includes dense coniferous forest where
detectability is very low, and therefore probably cannot really meet the
assumption that g(0)=1.  Does anyone have any suggestions on how to
address this?

Our current solution would be:
-left truncation
-using a larger bin of the first class
-fitting a function that hits f(0) at a presumed value

(We think that we have no responsive movement)

We would be grateful for any literature and suggestions
on the topic.

Thanks in advance,

Susan & Falk

R

messages.subject: Re: variance-covariance
messages.body_plain:
Sure.  The following is off the top of my head so you should work
through the delta method variances and covariances. I believe the
covariance term for a line transect example would be
n_i*n_j*var(f(0))/(L_i*L_j) assuming that the lines were randomly
selected so there is no covariance in the encounter rate between lines.
The diagonal variances are f(0)*f(0)*var(n_i/L_i) and you'll have to get
creative there because there is no empirical way of estimating the
variance from a single line.  You can probably take the combined
L^2*var(n/L)/n as an estimate of b and then use b*n_i/L_i^2 as the
estimate of the variance of the encounter rate for each line.  If you
are creating the v-c matrix for density then the above is missing
relevant constant terms and any aspect of average group size but that
should get you started in the right direction.  Steve do we have this
anywhere in the books?

--jeff

messages.subject: Evasive movement?
messages.body_plain:
I performed winter point counts using playback for Bachman's sparrows.
I had the highest number of responses occur 20-30 meters from the point.
Therefore my data lacks the "shoulder" at 0 and instead occurs in the
20-30m interval.  This implies that there is evasive movement or there
is simply lower response frequency within 20-30m perhaps because the
birds are "scared" of the playback.  I had more than 125 registrations
on each of two separate study sites(total ~250).  I am considering
setting the 20-30 meter interval as my "zero" then calculating the
densities to the "right" and then doing the same thing to the "left" and
adding the densities.  I have two questions 1) will this generate a
valid estimate? and 2) how do you add the variances if this can be done?
thanks,
clark jones

messages.subject: Re: Evasive movement?
messages.body_plain:
Clark-

Evasive movement is much less problematic than attractive movement in
generating bias. However, I'm not sure you have evasive movement.  With
point count data, a histogram of distances will have the interval with
the highest count at some distance from zero.  That is because the area
represented by the distance interval is increasing with the square of
distance (ie area of circle = pi*r*r).  At the same time the detection
probability decreases with distance, so the resulting histogram of
distances will increase and then decline.  I don't have the Intro
distance sampling book in front of me but I believe there is an
illustration of that in the book. That is why fit of the data to point
count is shown in 2 plots.  One shows the histogram of observed
distances as I've described and the other shows that histogram scaled to
represent a detection function which should have a shoulder.  You can
think about this latter histogram as representing observed distance in
each of the concentric rings represented by the distance intervals.  If
your email refers to this latter histogram you may have evasive movement
but I would not jump to that conclusion.  First I'd look at the
chi-square test to see if it suggested a lack of fit near distance 0.
Because the first distance interval represents a small area there is
much more variation in the number seen in that interval and a low number
does not imply a lack of fit necessarily.  Now if there is a lack of
fit, then you may want to consider evasive movement or other
explanations.  You offered 2 possible explanations and I'll offer a
third.  The best analytical solution will depend on the cause of the
problem.  If birds are scared and do not respond at close distance, then
your suggestion to truncate at 20-30m is the best way to go.  If
however, it is evasive movement and birds are moving from the close
interval to the 20-30m bin and then calling/seen, then you don't want to
truncate and you should fit the data as they are because it will smooth
those counts that are too high in the 20-30m bin and too low in the <20m
bin because of the evasive movement.  If you want further explanation of
that look back to the Wildlife Monograph of Burnham et al 1980 on line
transect sampling.  Now for a third possibility.  You are using playback
methods which I believe are fraught with problems.  See the work by
Klavitter on playback point counts with Hawaiian hawks.  I submit that
it may be just as likely that the bird is being attracted and that you
are first seeing them in the 20-30 m interval and they may represent
birds that were originally much further away.  This is a much more
insidious problem.  I submit that the only way you'll reconcile which is
the cause and the solution is to put transmitters on a sample of birds
and approach at various distances like the work of Klavitter.

Hope this helps.

--jeff

messages.subject: Re: Evasive movement?
messages.body_plain:
Further to Jeff's message (thanks Jeff), Steve Buckland and others have a
paper coming out in Journal of Applied Ecology about the use of playback
experiments in a distance-sampling-like framework.  A copy is on my web site
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/
under "Publications and preprints", and I've pasted the abstract below.

 - Len

Buckland, S.T., R.W. Summers, D.L. Borchers and L. Thomas. Point transect
sampling with traps or lures. Journal of Applied Ecology.

Summary
1. The ability to monitor abundance of animal populations is becoming
increasingly important, in light of growing concerns over the loss of
biodiversity through anthropogenic changes. A widely-used tool for such
monitoring is distance sampling, in which distances of detected animals from
a line or point are modelled, to estimate detectability and hence abundance.
Nevertheless, many species still prove problematic to survey. We develop two
extensions to point transect sampling that potentially allow abundance to be
estimated of a number of species from diverse taxa for which good survey
methods have not previously been available.
2. For each method, the primary survey comprises a random sample of points,
or more usually a systematic grid of points, through the region of interest.
Animals are lured to a point, or trapped at a point, and the number of
animals observed at each point is recorded. A separate study is conducted on
a subset of animals, to record whether they respond to the lure or enter the
trap, for a range of known distances from the point. These data are used to
estimate the probability that an animal will respond to the lure or enter
the trap, as a function of its initial distance from the point. This allows
the counts to be converted to an estimate of abundance in the survey region.
3. We illustrate the methods using a lure survey of crossbills Loxia spp. in
coniferous woodland in Scotland.
4. Synthesis and applications. Two extensions of point transect sampling
that use the same statistical methodology, lure point transects and trapping
point transects, are developed. Lure point transects extend the
applicability of distance sampling to species that can be lured to a point,
while trapping point transects potentially allow abundance estimation of
species that can be trapped, with fewer resources than are required by
trapping webs or conventional mark-recapture methods.

Key-words: distance sampling, logistic regression, Loxia scotica, lure point
transects, point transect sampling, trapping point transects, trapping webs

--

This topic reappears on the Distance list every couple of months:
please consult the archives of the list (which is searchable).  I repeat
my answer from November 2005 that references a further answer produced
in September of 2005

There have been a number of queries to this list about formatting
trapping web data for analysis in Program Distance.  The most recent
answer was provide by Dr. Thomas on 15 September of this year.
(http://www.jiscmail.ac.uk/cgi-bin/webadmin?A2=ind0509&L=DISTANCE-SAMPLING&P=R307&I=-3&X=4DBD493CEAC91402D7&Y=eri...%40mcs.st-and.ac.uk).

Entry of trapping web data is very similar to entry of point transect
data, as that is the method by which data are analysed to produce
density estimates.  There are 2 forms of inquiry that will be of
interest in getting entered into Distance:
1)  First, you should consult the sample projects that came with your
download of Distance.  Both the "house wren" and "songbird" sample
projects show data gathered from point transects, so their format are
applicable to the entry of trapping web data.  Note particularly the
recognition of no detections at a point transect (web) during a sampling
event.  This occurred on Point 5 of Region (stratum) 0 in the "house
wren" project, as well as Point 17 of Pasture 1 in 1980 in the
"songbird" project.  Note that there is no distance recorded associated
with the lack of detection (or capture).  Providing a distance of 0
implies an animal was detected at the sampling point (or centre of the
trapping web).

2)  You will want to acquaint yourself with entering distances in
intervals (also know as binned data).  Data from the sample projects I
describe above are all continuous data (ungrouped).  However, as your
traps are laid in concentric rings, distances are not continuous, but
rather constrained to the number of rings of traps you laid out.
Consult the section Miscellaneous CDS analysis topics in Chapter 8
Conventional distance sampling analysis,  of the Distance users guide
for a discussion of entering binned data.

messages.subject: Power Analysis Query
messages.body_plain:
Using Distance I have generated a population estimate for bottlenose
dolphin from a relatively small number of clustered sightings (n=47). The
estimate appears to be reasonable on the surface n = 139, but the
confidence intervals are quite large (74-182). A colleague suggested that
I might carry out a power analysis to establish how many sightings I would
need to calculate a population estimate with smaller confidence intervals.

My question is how would I do this using the results from Distance?

Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated,

Regards,

James Whiteford
Marine Researcher

--

messages.subject: Re: Power Analysis Query
messages.body_plain:
You don't need a power analysis.  You simply need to estimate the line
length that you need to achieve a specified level of precision.  You can
use the current data that you have to do that.  See chapter 7 of the
intro book.

--jeff

messages.subject_clean: significance testing & calculating unweighted global or
messages.body_plain:
From my take on it, you have a very simple solution because you have=20
estimated detection probability separately for the 2 mgmt units so
your mgmt unit estimates are independent. Thus all you really need is=20
the 2-sample t-test assuming unequal variances where each
sample is a management site. Remember that an ANOVA with 2 groups is=20
just a 2-sample t-test with
F=3Dt^2 but with the ANOVA you would have to assume equal variances for=20
most packages. Look in any
intro stats text and you'll find the formula for the test but you need=20
to keep in mind that the sample sizes are
most likely different for the 2 samples. I'm looking at Snedecor and=20
Cochran (which may not be in print any longer)
and the formula in terms of densities is

t=3D(D1 - D2)/sqrt( var(D1) + var(D2))

You get D1 and D2 from the output they are the densities from the 2=20
areas. You also get the standard errors for density and these need to be=20
squared (SE(D)*SE(D) =3D var(D)) to get the variance. If you look in many=
=20
texts it shows it as sqrt( s1^2/n1 +s2^2/n2) but what is output in=20
DISTANCE is equivalent to the std error of the mean which is=20
s1/sqrt(n1). Now the only other thing you need is the degrees of freedom=20
for the t-distribution but you probably have unequal sample sizes. The=20
solution that S&C suggest is to weight the degrees of freedom which is=20
similar to the Satterthwaite approximation we use to get the degrees of=20
freedom.

t'=3D(w1*t1+w2*t2)/(w1+w2) where w1=3Dvar(D1) and w2=3Dvar(D2) and t1 is =
the=20
significance value for df for D1 and t2 is the same for df from D2. Both=20
are output in DISTANCE. They can be non-integer values so you should=20
just round them up or down. If your t is >t' then the test is=20
significant at that alpha level. More importantly your estimate of the=20
density difference is D1-D2 and it's std error is sqrt( var(D1) + var(D2)=
).

Now if cv(D) is much beyond 0.20 (20%) then you should consider the log=20
transformation before doing the t-test. This just means using the ln(D)=20
in place of D and using cv^2 in place of var. See intro book for details.

Now to the question about whether you should weight or not in DISTANCE=20
by line length. Both the weighted and unweighted mean density by site=20
can be obtained (Len would know better how to do that) and both=20
variances are "valid" but typically we use the weighted mean because it=20
naturally weights the density values with the longest line which should=20
be the most precise. But I believe you can do both in DISTANCE depending=20
on your choice of how to weight the mean.

Hope this helps.

--jeff

estimates in section 3.6.5 of the introduction to distance sampling book.
As Jeff notes, it is easy in your case, because you are fitting separate
detection functions for the 2 mgt types.

Your 2nd solution should work if you want unweighted averages of the
transect-specific density estimates, but you made need to enter an area
corresponding to each transect - you could arbitrarily set each area to 1,
to ensure that the weights will be equal.

_______________________________________________________________________

To:           DISTANCE...@jiscmail.ac.uk
From:       David Anderson <ande...@cnr.colostate.edu>
Subject:   Significance tests for equality of management units in distance
sampling

Jeff Laake offers an effective technical solution to the question posed.  I
agree with his
insights and it is probably what I would have done until recently.

However, I want to offer an alternative,  Given the two management units,
say a and b,
we have the null hypothesis  Ho: Da = Db, where D is the true
density.  This is what
has been called a "silly null" as it is obviously false on a priori
grounds.  Of course
the null hypothesis is false -- do we really think that the density is
exactly the same
on two large management units?  I think everyone would agree the null is
false.

The alternative, from my perspective, is to just admit (assume) that the
two densities
are different and proceed to estimate the magnitude of the
difference.  This approach
asks a better question -- how big is the difference in density between the
two
management units?  Trivial? Small? Medium? Large? Very Large? So, this
difference
(an "effect size") can be estimated by taking the difference in the two
estimates,
Da-hat - Db-hat.  The sampling variance of this estimated difference is
just the
sum of the two variances (as Jeff explained).  An approximate 95 percent
confidence
interval is just the estimated difference plus or minus t*std error of the
difference,
where t is from the t-distribution, again, as Jeff explained.

This alternative will seem odd to many as the traditional -- null
hypothesis testing --
is so much a part of our DNA.  However, philosophically, I think the
estimation of
effect size and its precision is actually more informative.

David Anderson

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alexis, List,

Regarding your second question:

> >2) Because my transect lengths were not the same, my
> >stratum level (management type) density estimates are
> >averages across sites weighted by transect length.  I
> >would rather they be unweighted averages.  I can think

> >of two ways to do this, but I m uncertain about their

> >merits.  Will these approaches give a legitimate
> >standard error (and/or 95% confidence interval) for
> >the stratum density?

> >a) Generate sample-level density estimates using the
> >stratum detection function. Then, to create a
> >stratum-level density estimate with standard error,
> >average the sample estimates in the strata and
> >calculate their standard error.
> >b) Set up a separate DISTANCE project for each
> >management type, so that for each project the
> >management type is the global level, then designate
> >each transect as its own stratum (or, post-stratify at
> >the transect level), use a global detection function,
> >and specify that the global density estimate be

> >weighted by stratum area (a value which I won t enter,

> >so presumably, each sample would be given equal
> >weight).

Short answer:
Approach (a) will work, approach (b) will not.

Long answer:

Normally, when combining stratum estimates to produce a global estimate, one
asks whether the strata are fixed or random -- ie if you just want to make
inferences about those strata sampled (fixed effect), or about a larger
population of strata of which the ones you have data on are just a random
sample (random effect).  If fixed, the appropriate variance is a weighted
average of the stratum-level variance estimates.  If random, the appropriate
variance is calculated from the variation between transect estimates (and
doesn't use the estimates of variance from each transect).

When you tell Distance to estimate density as the mean of the stratum
estimates, weighted by area (in the Estimate tab of the model definition),
it assumes the strata are fixed.  When you tell it to estimate density as
the mean of stratum estimates, weighted by effort (line length) it gives you
the option to assume the strata are fixed or random -- there is a "strata
are replicates" box you tick to tell it the strata are random.  The reason
it doesn't allow random strata for area-weighted analyses (or no weighting)
is largely historical.

You can find out more about these various options by looking in the online
help -- search for "replicates" and choose the topic "Estimate Tab - CDS and
MCDS".

In your case, you have to assume that the 87 sites are random samples from a
larger population of possible sites.  You don't have any replicate lines on
each site, so you can't calculate site-specific variances of encounter rate
and thus density estimates, so you can't calculate an average of these
variances to get the variance of an overall estimate of density as one would
want to if you assume the sites are fixed.  Anyway, you probably were
thinking of the sites as random effects.  So, you want to calculate variance
in density using the variation in density estimates between sites.  I'm
afraid the only way to do this is manually, as you suggested.  Predict
density by sample (ie by site, since you only have one line per site), put
these into another package and calculate the unweighted mean and variance by
management category.  Rather than typing in all the density estimates, you
might find it easier get Distance to save the stats file, and import them
from there.  The stats file is documented in the MCDS engine reference
appendix (I'm assuming you're using Distance 5 -- I think the documentation

messages.subject: comparing densities across habitats and years
messages.subject_clean: comparing densities across habitats and years
messages.body_plain:
Hi list,

I'm using Distance 5 to compare bird species densities between burned and
unburned pine forest generated from 30 randomized 15-point transects in each
habitat.  I have 5 yrs of data from the burned site (2001-2005) and 4 yrs
from the surrounding unburned forest (missing 2004).  I've decided that the
simplest and perhaps most meaningful way to relate the abundance of species
between the two habitats is to compare the average densities across the 5-yr
period from each habitat.  But it is also interesting to examine changes in
species' density within each habitat over the 5-yr period, especially in the
burn, so I am also interested in obtaining within-year estimates of density
for each species in each habitat.  For these analyses I put all the data
from both habitats into a single project, and I am treating habitat and year
both as region-level strata, I have put observers and the point transects in
the point transect layer, and the counts along each transect, along with all
the related bird data, in the observation layer.  My data filter selects one
species from one habitat, and I am using the MCDS engine so that I can also
examine effects of observers (but likely only across species and within
years, due to relatively few detections by individual observers for each
species in a given year).  In the estimate tab of the data filter I am
post-stratifying estimates by year, and under "level of resolution of
estimates" I have ticked global and strata (year) estimates for density, and
then only strata estimates for encounter rate, detection function, and
cluster size.  My global density estimate is a mean of the strata estimates,
weighted by total effort in each strata, as the total number of counts along
the transects varied a bit from year to year ("strata are replicates" is NOT
ticked).  I am running separate analyses for half-normal cosine and
hazard-rate simple polynomial models, visually examining the detection
functions and probability plots for fit and truncation points, and selecting
the best model mainly based on AIC of the global estimate.

I am interested to hear feedback on whether this seems like the right
approach for this type of comparison, and whether all the steps I have taken
are appropriate.

Also, I am interested to hear your opinions on whether using a global
detection function (across years, within habitat) is better for generating a
density estimate for a species in year when detections of that species were
very few, or whether it is best to maintain independent detection functions
across years, regardless of sample size (so long as the warning "Number of
observations is small. Do not expect reasonable results" does not appear in
the log). But, even when such a warning appears, if the data fit the line
very tightly in the Qq plot, is it still best to pool across years for a
detection function, or would it be better to maintain independent detection
functions?

Thanks much for your help,

Arvind Panjabi

Rocky Mountain Bird Observatory

messages.subject: Trapping Web for Fish in Wetland Situation
messages.subject_clean: Trapping Web for Fish in Wetland Situation
messages.body_plain:
Dear List:

I have a need to develop a sampling method to collect density and diversity
data of fishes from shallow wetlands of the Florida Everglades.  We will be
conducting an extensive foodweb study and need population-level data of
small fish (<80mm) and crayfish in treatment and control plots.

Initially, I conceived of using a Capture-Recapture method, but after
extensive review and testing, we cannot individually mark these fish
because they are too small.  We must batch-mark all animals we catch by fin
nicking.  This to me negates the ability to conduct most Capture-Recapture
techniques.

Given our limitations, I believe that a Trapping Web could be useful to
collect our needed density and diversity information.  We will be employing
passive samplers to collect fish over several days (minnow traps).  In
addition, we will be surrounding our study area by a drift fence to
prohibit gains/losses of animals.  Coupled with our short sampling
timeframe, this should satisfy the closed-population requirement.

The Trapping Web has 3 necessary assumptions (see Buckland et al. 1993):
all center animals are captured, no migration & small relative movements,
and accurate trap distance measurements.

I believe we can satisfy most of these conditions; however, we have a
limited amount of information about these fish movements, but believe the
range is small within a few days.

The help I am seeking would be any field stories or examples whereby the
Trapping Web was used, 1) in an aquatic situation for fishes and/or 2) if
this indeed is the MOST appropriate assessment technique for our situation,
and if not 3) please let us know what analytical technique you believe
would be more robust, etc.

Best regards,

Mac Kobza

Aquatic Ecologist
Everglades Division
South Florida Water Management District
rko...@sfwmd.gov

messages.subject_clean: comparing densities across habitats and years
messages.body_plain:
Hi Arvind, list,

Sounds just-about fine to me.  A few points:

- I wasn't clear whether you were clear that you can't compare AICs among
models with different truncation points.  You have to choose your truncation
point first, and then do the model selection.

- The "do not expect reasonable results" warning occurs if you try to fit a
detection function with fewer than 10 points.  In fact, you are unlikely to
get reasonable results even with rather more than this -- the Intro to
Distance book recommends between 90 and 120 observations for point transect
analyses I think -- however you can reliable detection function estimates from
fewer if the true detection function has a wide shoulder.  For example, I've
seen well-known authorities on distance sampling publish papers with point
transect detection functions fit to 44 observations
(see http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf)

- One minor problem with the estimates of variance of density for each habitat
(pooled over years) is that presumably the same transects were sampled each
year.  Distance assumes that the encounter rate estimates in each year are
independent.  This is not a major problem in practice, as with a sample size
of points as large as yours it won't make much difference if you re-do the
analysis but respecting the repeated nature of the data.  However, if you want
to do it exactly right, you could bootstrap the data, resampling transects.
If you select a transect in year 1 you would also select that same transect in
the other years.  I think I've posted about this kind of analysis before --
try searching the archives for "bootstrap".  You can't do it within Distance
-- instead you'd need to write a short program in another language to
bootstrap the data and call the MCDS.exe program to estimate density for each
resample.  A grad student here, Tiago Marques, has some template code to do
this kind of analysis.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.body_plain:
Steve Buckland has corrected me on the following:

>> >> get reasonable results even with rather more than this -- the Intro to
>> >> Distance book recommends between 90 and 120 observations for point transect
>> >> analyses I think -- however you can reliable detection function estimates

On p241 of the book we say 75-100 for point transects (on p240 we say 60-80
for line transects).

Serves me right for being too lazy to look it up.

However, remember this is just a rough guide -- for example, one can get away
with a smaller sample size if the detection function shoulder is wide
(relative to the truncation width).  On the other hand, if the detection
function has a strong "spike" close to zero, then one is unlikely to get a
reliable result even for a rather larger sample size.

 - Len

Hi Silka, list,

I was able to reproduce the problem you report in Distance 4.1 release 2, but
not in Distance 5.0 Beta 5 (the latest beta).  So, I guess it's an example of
a problem I've fixed without even knowing it was there!  It only occurs in
D4.1 when you estimate density by sample, stratum and globally, and I wasn't
clear why you need density by sample, so one option is to turn that off.  The
other is to upgrade to D5.0.

Cheers,

 - Len
